introduction: Everything in the world moves in cycles, these passages say: seed and tree, the seasons, the rise and fall of peoples, the worlds themselves. They use that pattern to explain religion. Each Manifestation of God brings a spring; summer, autumn and winter follow; and a new spring comes, not as the same flowers but as the same kind. They also draw comfort from it, since winter storms are what make the spring. Sixty-six outside voices stand beside them: Ecclesiastes and the Psalms on return and passing, the Gospels on seed and season, the Qur’an on the earth revived, the Gita on ages, Heraclitus and Marcus Aurelius, Boethius, Shakespeare and Shelley, with Job, Khayyam and Yeats for what does not come back.
questions: "These flowers are the return of last year's flowers." In what sense? What returns, and what does not, according to these passages?
The Preacher says there is nothing new under the sun; a talk here says that what is renewed is in a better condition. Is history in these readings a circle or something else?
How is the image of the four seasons used to explain why a religion needs renewal? What would a critic say the image leaves out?
Job says there is hope for a felled tree but not for a man; Shakespeare's seven ages end in oblivion. Do the cycles described here hold any comfort for an individual life?
Ten passages say that without winter there is no spring. When has that been true in your experience, and when does it sound too easy?
Shelley's chorus asks whether hate and death must return with the golden age. What do these passages answer?

outside.why: After the flood Genesis promises that seedtime and harvest, summer and winter, day and night shall not cease.
The Preacher watches generations, the sun, the wind and the rivers go round and return to their place.
Peter speaks of times of refreshing and of a restoration of all things, of which the prophets spoke.
Jesus tells of a fig tree that bore no fruit, and of the dresser who asked for one more year to dig about it.
Jesus says that new wine is put into new bottles, and that an old garment will not bear a new patch.
Job says that a tree cut down may sprout again at the scent of water, but a man lies down and does not rise. Is the renewal described here a comfort to the old tree, or only to the garden?
FitzGerald's Omar says that the moving finger writes and moves on, and nothing lures it back. What returns with this year's roses, and what does not?
Paul says that the seed sown is not the body that shall be, but bare grain, and that it must die to live.
Jesus says that a grain of wheat bears much fruit only if it falls into the ground and dies.
The Qur’an says that God brings the living from the dead and the dead from the living, and revives the earth after its death.
Boethius sings that all things yearn for their due return, and that nothing keeps its order unless its end is joined to its beginning.

Marcus Aurelius held that all things come round in a circle and are of like forms from eternity. How does the distinction here between the return of the kind and the return of the individual alter his picture?
Jesus calls himself the true vine and his Father the gardener, who tends the branches for fruit.
A psalm says to God: thou sendest forth thy spirit, and thou renewest the face of the earth.
Emerson held that every natural fact is a symbol of some spiritual fact.
Krishna says that whenever righteousness declines he comes again, from age to age.
Shelley sings that the world's great age begins anew and the golden years return.
The Qur’an makes night and day, sun and moon a sign, each keeping to its measured course.
Jesus tells his disciples to learn from the fig tree: when its branch is tender, summer is near.
The Gita speaks of ages at whose close all things return to the divine being, and at whose beginning they are sent forth again.
A psalm says that heaven and earth will wear out like a garment and be changed, while God remains the same.
Yeats also thought in great cycles, and saw his own turning as a gyre widening until the centre could not hold. What does the close of a cycle look like in this passage?
Paul says that the night is far spent and the day is at hand.
Shelley's traveller finds of a great king's works a broken statue and level sand.
Isaiah says that all flesh is grass that withers, and that the word of God stands for ever.
A psalm says that a man's days are as grass, and that the mercy of God is from everlasting to everlasting.
This is the verse of the Qur’an that the passage echoes: thou wilt not find any change in God's way.
Shakespeare likens our minutes to waves making toward the shore, each changing place with the one before.
Heraclitus said that no one steps twice into the same river, for fresh waters are always flowing in.
Tennyson's Arthur says that the old order changes, yielding place to new.
Shakespeare sees his own autumn in boughs where late the sweet birds sang. What can be said to a person in the season of decline?
Jaques counts the ages of a life and ends in second childishness and mere oblivion, with no spring after. Is the cycle of a human life like the cycle of a dynasty or a tree?
Kipling reminded an empire at its height that its pomp might be one with Nineveh and Tyre.
The first letter of John says that the world passes away, and its desire.
Hamlet traces how a king may go a progress through the body of a beggar.
Whitman bequeaths himself to the dirt, to grow from the grass he loves.
Rumi tells the same journey through mineral, plant and animal to man, and beyond.
Heraclitus said that the way up and the way down are one and the same.
The Revelation of John hears from the throne: behold, I make all things new.
Shakespeare's Edmund mocks the habit of blaming the sun, moon and stars for our own disasters.
The Qur’an says that God causes good and bad days to follow one another among mankind.
Daniel blesses the God who changes the times and the seasons, and removes kings and sets them up.

The Preacher says that what has been is what shall be, and that there is nothing new under the sun. He says it wearily. Another passage here says that what is renewed is found in a better condition. Circle, or spiral?
This is the passage of Ecclesiastes quoted, in the words of the King James Bible.
The Qur’an says that for every period there is a book, and for everything a time prescribed.
Lamentations says that the mercies of God do not fail and are new every morning.
Proverbs describes a neglected field, grown over with thorns, its wall broken down.
The book of Judges tells how a generation arose that did not know what had been done for its fathers.
The Qur’an says: know that God gives life to the earth after its death.
Herbert asks who would have thought his shrivelled heart could have recovered greenness.
Shelley's chorus of a returning golden age ends in dread: must hate and death return too? If the spring comes round, must the winter?
Isaiah says that the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light.
The Qur’an says: as We began the first creation, We shall repeat it.
A psalm says that those who sow in tears shall reap in joy.
Shelley calls the wind of autumn destroyer and preserver, driving the dead leaves and bearing the seeds.
The letter of James points to the farmer who waits with patience for the early and the latter rain.
Isaiah says that rain and snow come down and do not return until they have made the earth bring forth.
Shelley ends his ode with the question these letters answer: if winter comes, can spring be far behind?
Paul says that tribulation works patience, and patience experience, and experience hope.
A psalm says that weeping may endure for a night, but joy comes in the morning.
Hopkins tells a child grieving over falling leaves that it is herself she mourns for. What is it in us that the autumn touches?
Job says of the same giving and taking: the Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away.
A psalm hears day speaking to day and night to night, without end.
Isaiah foretells that the desert shall rejoice and blossom as the rose.
The Song of Songs says: the winter is past, the rain is over and gone, the flowers appear on the earth.
Paul speaks of a moment when the dead are raised and all are changed.

matthew-new-wine-old-bottles.text: No man putteth a piece of new cloth unto an old garment, for that which is put in to fill it up taketh from the garment, and the rent is made worse. Neither do men put new wine into old bottles: else the bottles break, and the wine runneth out, and the bottles perish: but they put new wine into new bottles, and both are preserved

acts-times-of-refreshing.text: Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord. And he shall send Jesus Christ, which before was preached unto you: Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began

matthew-parable-of-the-fig-tree.text: Now learn a parable of the fig tree; When his branch is yet tender, and putteth forth leaves, ye know that summer is nigh: So likewise ye, when ye shall see all these things, know that it is near, even at the doors

proverbs-field-of-the-slothful.text: I went by the field of the slothful, and by the vineyard of the man void of understanding; And, lo, it was all grown over with thorns, and nettles had covered the face thereof, and the stone wall thereof was broken down. Then I saw, and considered it well: I looked upon it, and received instruction

psalm-days-are-as-grass.text: As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth. For the wind passeth over it, and it is gone; and the place thereof shall know it no more. But the mercy of the Lord is from everlasting to everlasting upon them that fear him, and his righteousness unto children's children

ecclesiastes-sun-also-ariseth.text: One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever. The sun also ariseth, and the sun goeth down, and hasteth to his place where he arose. The wind goeth toward the south, and turneth about unto the north; it whirleth about continually, and the wind returneth again according to his circuits. All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full; unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again

quran-quickeneth-the-earth-after-its-dea.text: Know that Allah quickeneth the earth after its death. We have made clear Our revelations for you, that haply ye may understand.

quran-vicissitudes.text: If ye have received a blow, the (disbelieving) people have received a blow the like thereof. These are (only) the vicissitudes which We cause to follow one another for mankind, to the end that Allah may know those who believe and may choose witnesses from among you; and Allah loveth not wrong-doers.

quran-for-everything-a-time-prescribed.text: And verily We sent messengers (to mankind) before thee, and We appointed for them wives and offspring, and it was not (given) to any messenger that he should bring a portent save by Allah's leave. For everything there is a time prescribed.

quran-no-change-in-allahs-way.text: (Shown in their) behaving arrogantly in the land and plotting evil; and the evil plot encloseth but the men who make it. Then, can they expect aught save the treatment of the folk of old? Thou wilt not find for Allah's way of treatment any substitute, nor wilt thou find for Allah's way of treatment aught of power to change.

quran-as-we-began-the-first-creation.text: The Day when We shall roll up the heavens as a recorder rolleth up a written scroll. As We began the first creation, We shall repeat it. (It is) a promise (binding) upon Us. Lo! We are to perform it.

quran-earth-barren-then-it-thrills.text: O mankind! if ye are in doubt concerning the Resurrection, then lo! We have created you from dust, then from a drop of seed, then from a clot, then from a little lump of flesh shapely and shapeless, that We may make (it) clear for you. And We cause what We will to remain in the wombs for an appointed time, and afterward We bring you forth as infants, then (give you growth) that ye attain your full strength. And among you there is he who dieth (young), and among you there is he who is brought back to the most abject time of life, so that, after knowledge, he knoweth naught. And thou (Muhammad) seest the earth barren, but when We send down water thereon, it doth thrill and swell and put forth every lovely kind (of growth).

quran-they-float-each-in-an-orbit.text: A token unto them is night. We strip it of the day, and lo! they are in darkness. And the sun runneth on unto a resting-place for him. That is the measuring of the Mighty, the Wise. And for the moon We have appointed mansions till she return like an old shrivelled palm-leaf. It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor doth the night outstrip the day. They float each in an orbit

marcus-come-round-in-a-circle.text: all things from eternity are of like forms and come round in a circle
marcus-come-round-in-a-circle.author: Marcus Aurelius

shelley-must-hate-and-death-return.text: must hate and death return? / Cease! must men kill and die? / Cease! drain not to its dregs the urn / Of bitter prophecy! / The world is weary of the past— / O might it die or rest at last
shelley-must-hate-and-death-return.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley

shakespeare-that-time-of-year.text: That time of year thou mayst in me behold / When yellow leaves, or none, or few, do hang / Upon those boughs which shake against the cold, / Bare ruin'd choirs, where late the sweet birds sang
shakespeare-that-time-of-year.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

shakespeare-like-as-the-waves.text: Like as the waves make towards the pebbled shore, / So do our minutes hasten to their end; / Each changing place with that which goes before, / In sequent toil all forwards do contend
shakespeare-like-as-the-waves.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)
